stimulus.text: Historian James McPherson notes that Americans in 1861 expected 'a short, glorious war' — yet the conflict dragged on for four years because 'the South's will to resist and the North's need to conquer an entire society made anything swift impossible.'

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE reason the Civil War lasted longer than people initially expected.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND reason it lasted so long.
C. Briefly explain ONE important turning point of the war.
exemplar: Both sides entered expecting a short war, but new rifled weapons and entrenched positions made battles far bloodier and less decisive than anyone imagined.
The Confederacy's vast territory meant the Union had to conquer and occupy an area the size of Western Europe while maintaining a 3,500-mile blockade — a task that took four years.
Gettysburg and Vicksburg (July 1863) marked the turning point: Lee's invasion of the North failed and Grant seized the Mississippi, splitting the Confederacy.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of Progressive action to reform the American economy.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of Progressive economic reform.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of Progressive action to reform American politics.
exemplar: Reform mayors like Cleveland's Tom Johnson municipalized utilities to give citizens cheaper, better service, while governors like Wisconsin's La Follette regulated railroads and pushed direct primaries.
At the federal level, Roosevelt's trust-busting and the Hepburn Act (1906) strengthened railroad regulation, and the Pure Food and Drug and Meat Inspection Acts protected consumers.
Politically, Progressives pushed direct democracy: the initiative, referendum, recall, direct election of senators (Seventeenth Amendment), and women's suffrage (Nineteenth Amendment).

stimulus.text: The table shows voter participation in presidential elections: 1824 — about 27% of eligible voters cast ballots; 1828 — about 58%; 1840 — about 80%. The sharp rise coincides with the elimination of property qualifications for voting in most states during the Jacksonian era.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE way Andrew Jackson fostered the growth of 'Jacksonian democracy.'
B. Briefly explain a SECOND way he fostered it.
C. Briefly explain ONE policy promoted by Jackson's political opponents.
exemplar: Jackson championed the expansion of white male suffrage: property qualifications for voting fell across the states, and the 'common man' entered politics as never before.
Jackson's victory in the disputed election of 1828 — after the 'corrupt bargain' of 1824 — was hailed as the triumph of the people's will over entrenched elites.
Jackson's opponents, the National Republicans and later Whigs, promoted Clay's American System: a national bank, protective tariffs, and federally funded internal improvements.
